data.title: Design Facebook Messenger
data.contentPreview:
## 1. What is Facebook Messenger?

Facebook Messenger is a realtime communication product for 1:1 chats and small group conversations across phones and web clients. What feels simple in the UI hides a harder backend problem: message history must stay authoritative and ordered, while presence, read receipts, notifications, and multi-device delivery all depend on low-latency but lossy infrastructure around that durable core.

## 2. Requirements

Messenger-style chat should feel instant on every device, yet the only story users can trust after a crash is the ordered conversation history. Presence, live pushes, and read hints are fast layers around that durable core, not a second source of truth.

### Clarifying Questions

::::qa-item
:::you[You]
"Is there a hard cap on how many people can be in a single group conversation, or do we need to handle groups with hundreds or thousands of members?"
:::
:::interviewer[Interviewer]
"Group conversations are capped at roughly `250` members. Messenger is built for personal communication, not broadcast. The dominant shape is 1:1 and small groups."
:::
:::takeaway[Takeaway]
The bounded group size is a key simplifying constraint. Small-group fan-out stays manageable in the synchronous send path, unlike large-channel delivery that would require a fundamentally different delivery model.
:::
::::

::::qa-item
:::you[You]
"If I add someone to a group conversation that has been going for a while, can that new member read everything that was said before they joined, or only messages sent after they were added?"
:::
:::interviewer[Interviewer]
"New members can read the full conversation history by default. This is not something individual conversations can configure."
:::
:::takeaway[Takeaway]
Membership semantics are full shared history rather than from-join-only visibility. A newly added member's device will load all prior messages on first open, and any group-scoped history cache must not be filtered by join timestamp.
:::
::::

::::qa-item
:::you[You]
"What is the latency target for the send confirmation? And if two people in the same conversation send messages at nearly the same moment, do those messages need to appear in the same order on every device?"
:::
:::interviewer[Interviewer]
"Target `p95` under `200 ms` for the durable send acknowledgment. Within a single conversation, messages must appear in the same order on every device regardless of who sent them or which device they came from."
:::
:::takeaway[Takeaway]
The send ACK requires durable commit with a server-assigned sequence before the caller is unblocked. Sequence allocation is per-conversation, so independent conversations are fully decoupled and a global ordering is not required.
:::
::::
